title: Who are we
hookLine: in British Punjab, Sikhs asked what made Sikhi distinct

lines: AROUND THE FIRE, OR THE GURU?
A SMALL ARGUMENT, A BIG QUESTION.
cards: A wedding is being planned in a Punjab village. The families are Sikh. Should the couple walk around a sacred fire, as their Hindu neighbors do and as their own grandparents did?
Or around the Guru Granth Sahib, while the Lavan hymns are sung? An uncle says one thing, a cousin back from Lahore says another, and the bride's mother just wants everyone to stop shouting.
A small family argument, about a very big question.

teach.b: Without a Sikh kingdom, with missionaries preaching and reformers arguing, Sikhs found themselves asking something they'd once taken for granted: what actually makes a Sikh a Sikh? The questions got very practical.

teach.h: WHICH WEDDING, WHICH NAMES, WHAT HAIR?
teach.b: Which wedding rite. Which names. Whether to keep the hair uncut.
Whether caste customs belonged in the Guru's house. Some Sikhs had taken amrit, some kept uncut hair without it, some cut their hair and still called themselves followers of Guru Nanak.
Two answers were sincerely held. Some Sikhs saw Sikhi as living inside a wider Hindu world, sharing many festivals, customs and shrines with their neighbors, and saw no reason to draw sharp lines.
Others argued that the Gurus had given the Sikhs their own scripture, their own rites and their own form, and that Sikhi stood on its own. Both sides loved the Gurus.
They disagreed about what loving them required, and these lessons don't pick a winner.
Guru Arjan, in a hymn in Raag Bhairo, says he is neither Hindu nor Muslim, and that his body and his breath belong to the One who is called both Allah and Ram.
Sikhs on both sides of the argument read that hymn, and drew different things from it.
The question didn't get one answer in a day. Next come the answers people built: societies, schools, books, a law about weddings. But it began with a family around a table, asking.

how: Sikhs today still discuss what marks a Sikh, and the Sikh Rehat Maryada, the code of conduct, sets out the Sikh wedding around the Guru Granth Sahib with the Lavan hymns.

o: the wedding hymns sung as a couple circles the Guru
a sacred fire a couple walks around to marry

s: in British Punjab, all Sikhs agreed on what made a Sikh
some saw Sikhi inside a wider Hindu world; others argued it stood on its own.
the argument reached into weddings, names and hair
the big question showed up in very practical choices.

games.q: you're at the family table. a cousin says Sikhs should marry only around the Guru Granth Sahib; an uncle says the old fire rite is fine. what happened in Punjab, as the histories tell it?
o: Sikhs argued it out for years, and built answers.
games.why: Sikhs argued it out, sincerely, on both sides, and the answers they built (societies, schools, books, a law about weddings) come next in the story.

practice: Let one question rest in you for a while: what makes me me?

Not your job title or your phone, but something deeper, a value you won't trade, a habit you keep even when nobody's watching, a place or a people you belong to; let a few answers come and go, and notice which one stays.
If you pray, hold that answer before Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Lavan, the wedding hymns sung as a couple circles the Guru Granth Sahib: one sign of the question Sikhs asked about what made Sikhi distinct. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: neither Hindu nor Muslim. Both sides of the argument read the same hymn. Nine hundred fifty-three days, and counting.
